source.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר שְׁמוּאֵל֙ אֶל־שָׁא֔וּל אֹתִ֨י שָׁלַ֤ח יְהוָה֙ לִמְשָׁחֳךָ֣ לְמֶ֔לֶךְ עַל־עַמּ֖וֹ עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וְעַתָּ֣ה שְׁמַ֔ע לְק֖וֹל דִּבְרֵ֥י יְהוָֽה׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And said Samuel to Saul, me sent Yahweh to anoint you as king over his people, over Israel; and now listen to [the] voice of [the] words of Yahweh.

en.L: And Samuel said to Saul, "Me {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} sent to anoint you as king over {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} people, over Israel. And now, listen to the voice of the words of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.B: Samuel said to Saul, "I am the one {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} sent to anoint you king over {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} people Israel. So now, listen to what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} is saying.
en.R: Samuel said to Saul, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} sent me to anoint you as king over {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} people Israel. So now listen to the message from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: me the LORD sent: Samuel stresses that he is the one God sent
decisions.reason: The word "me" stands first in the sentence for emphasis. Samuel reminds Saul that it was through him that the LORD made Saul king (9:16; 10:1), so the command he is about to pass on carries the same authority as that anointing.

decisions.choice: listen to the voice of the words of the LORD: hear and do what he says
alternatives: obey the words of the LORD
decisions.reason: To "listen to the voice" of someone is to obey them. The phrase opens the question the whole chapter turns on: whether Saul will listen to the LORD (verses 19, 20, 22) or to the people (verse 24).

decisions.choice: I am the one the LORD sent (Balanced); listen to what the LORD is saying / the message from the LORD
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the stress on "me" (m1) with "I am the one"; Readable uses the plain order. Both levels give "the voice of the words" as what the LORD is saying, and keep "listen", since the chapter builds on that word (m2).

source.text: כֹּ֤ה אָמַר֙ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֔וֹת פָּקַ֕דְתִּי אֵ֛ת אֲשֶׁר־עָשָׂ֥ה עֲמָלֵ֖ק לְיִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל אֲשֶׁר־שָׂ֥ם לוֹ֙ בַּדֶּ֔רֶךְ בַּעֲלֹת֖וֹ מִמִּצְרָֽיִם׃

records.literal_gloss: Thus says Yahweh of hosts, I have taken note of what did Amalek to Israel, how he set against him on the way when he came up from Egypt.

en.L: Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of hosts: I have taken note of what Amalek did to Israel, how he set [himself] against him on the way when he came up from Egypt.
en.B: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies says this: I have taken note of what Amalek did to Israel, how they opposed Israel on the road as Israel came up out of Egypt.
en.R: This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies says: I have not forgotten what the Amalekites did to Israel. They attacked the Israelites on the road when they were coming up out of Egypt.

decisions.choice: I have taken note of: I have marked it and will call it to account
decisions.reason: The verb means to pay attention to, to visit. Used of a wrong that was done, it means to hold someone to account for it (Exodus 20:5; 32:34). The LORD has not forgotten, and the command that follows carries out his sentence.

decisions.choice: what Amalek did: the attack on Israel in the wilderness
alternatives: how he laid an ambush for him on the way
decisions.reason: Amalek attacked Israel at Rephidim soon after the exodus (Exodus 17:8-16), striking the weary people at the rear (Deuteronomy 25:17-19). The LORD swore to blot out the memory of Amalek, and Deuteronomy charged Israel to do it once the people had rest in the land. Saul is now sent to carry out that old sentence.

decisions.choice: the LORD of hosts: the LORD who commands the armies of heaven and earth
decisions.reason: "Hosts" means armies. The title, first used in this book at 1:3, presents the LORD as the commander of every power. It fits a word that sends Israel to war at his order.

decisions.choice: the LORD of Armies; The LORD of Armies says this (Balanced); This is what the LORD of Armies says (Readable)
decisions.reason: As across Samuel and Kings, Literal keeps "the LORD of hosts" and Balanced and Readable say "Armies", the plain sense of "hosts" (m3). The messenger formula follows the same book-wide wording at each level.

decisions.choice: they, Israel (Balanced); I have not forgotten, the Amalekites (Readable)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew speaks of each nation as "he". Balanced and Readable use plural forms and name Israel where "him" would be unclear. Readable says "I have not forgotten" for "I have taken note" (m1), and "attacked" for "set against", as the events of Exodus 17:8 were.

source.text: עַתָּה֩ לֵ֨ךְ וְהִכִּֽיתָ֜ה אֶת־עֲמָלֵ֗ק וְהַֽחֲרַמְתֶּם֙ אֶת־כָּל־אֲשֶׁר־ל֔וֹ וְלֹ֥א תַחְמֹ֖ל עָלָ֑יו וְהֵמַתָּ֞ה מֵאִ֣ישׁ עַד־אִשָּׁ֗ה מֵֽעֹלֵל֙ וְעַד־יוֹנֵ֔ק מִשּׁ֣וֹר וְעַד־שֶׂ֔ה מִגָּמָ֖ל וְעַד־חֲמֽוֹר׃ס

records.literal_gloss: Now go and strike Amalek, and devote to destruction all that [is] to him, and not spare him; and put to death from man to woman, from child and to nursing [one], from ox and to sheep, from camel and to donkey.

en.L: Now go and strike Amalek, and devote to destruction all that he has, and do not spare him. And put [them] to death, from man to woman, from child to nursing infant, from ox to sheep, from camel to donkey."
en.B: Now go and strike Amalek. Devote to destruction everything they have, and do not spare them. Put them to death, men and women, children and nursing infants, cattle and sheep, camels and donkeys."
en.R: Now go and attack the Amalekites. Destroy them completely, with everything they have, as given over to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. Do not spare them. Kill men and women, children and babies, cattle and sheep, camels and donkeys."

decisions.choice: devote to destruction: give over wholly to the LORD by destroying
decisions.reason: This is the verb behind the "devoted thing" of Leviticus 27:28-29, explained at Deuteronomy 7:2: what is devoted is taken out of human use and handed over to the LORD for good. In war it means the enemy is destroyed and nothing is kept for private gain (Joshua 6:17-19). The same word runs through this chapter (verses 8, 9, 15, 18, 20, 21), and the story turns on what Saul kept back.

decisions.choice: the ban on Amalek: the LORD's sentence on Amalek's attack, carried out by Israel
decisions.reason: This is one of the hardest commands in Scripture. The note at Deuteronomy 7:2 sets out what the Law itself says about such commands. Here the reason given is not the land or its worship but what Amalek had done: they had attacked Israel on the way out of Egypt, preying on the weak and weary (verse 2; Exodus 17:8-16; Deuteronomy 25:17-19), and the LORD had sworn to bring their memory to an end. Verse 18 calls them "the sinners". The command is the LORD's, not Saul's: it was not to be used for gain, and the chapter faults Saul for keeping the best for himself and his people (verses 9, 19). The text states the command as it was given. Amalekites still appear later in the book (27:8; 30:1), so the verse does not by itself settle how fully it was carried out or how its language of war is to be weighed.

decisions.choice: you (one person) ... you (many): Saul and his army
decisions.reason: Most of the verbs speak to Saul alone, but "devote to destruction" is plural. The command is given to Saul as king, and it binds the army that carries it out with him, which is why the people share the blame in verses 9, 15 and 21.

decisions.choice: from man to woman ... from camel to donkey: every person and every animal
decisions.reason: Pairs joined by "from ... to" name the two ends of a range to mean everything in it. Nothing living was to be kept, which rules out taking the herds as plunder (compare verse 9).

decisions.choice: destroy them completely, as given over to the LORD
decisions.reason: As at Deuteronomy 7:2, Readable gives the sense of the term in plain words: the Amalekites were to be destroyed because they were given over to the LORD, not taken for gain. Literal and Balanced keep "devote to destruction".

decisions.choice: they, them
decisions.reason: The Hebrew speaks of Amalek as "him", one nation. Literal keeps it; Balanced and Readable use the plural, since the command concerns a whole people.

source.text: וַיְשַׁמַּ֤ע שָׁאוּל֙ אֶת־הָעָ֔ם וַֽיִּפְקְדֵם֙ בַּטְּלָאִ֔ים מָאתַ֥יִם אֶ֖לֶף רַגְלִ֑י וַעֲשֶׂ֥רֶת אֲלָפִ֖ים אֶת־אִ֥ישׁ יְהוּדָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And summoned Saul the people and mustered them at Telaim: two hundred thousand foot soldiers, and ten thousand men of Judah.

en.L: And Saul summoned the people and mustered them at Telaim, 200,000 foot soldiers, and 10,000 men of Judah.
en.B: So Saul called up the army and mustered them at Telaim: 200,000 foot soldiers, and 10,000 men from Judah.
en.R: So Saul called the army together at Telaim and counted them. There were 200,000 soldiers on foot, and 10,000 men from Judah.

decisions.choice: the people: the fighting men called up for war
decisions.reason: "The people" often means the army gathered for battle (11:11; 14:17). In this chapter "the people" are Saul's troops (verses 9, 15, 21, 24).

decisions.choice: Telaim: a place in the south of Judah
decisions.reason: The place is named only here. It is probably the Telem of Joshua 15:24, a town in the Negev of Judah, near the lands where Amalek roamed.

decisions.choice: and 10,000 men of Judah: Judah counted on its own
decisions.reason: As in 11:8, the men of Judah are counted apart from the rest of Israel. On the size of numbers counted in "thousands", see the note at Numbers 1:21.

decisions.choice: called up the army (Balanced); called the army together (Readable)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "summoned the people"; Balanced and Readable say what "the people" are here (m1).

source.text: וַיָּבֹ֥א שָׁא֖וּל עַד־עִ֣יר עֲמָלֵ֑ק וַיָּ֖רֶב בַּנָּֽחַל׃

records.literal_gloss: And came Saul to [the] city of Amalek and lay in wait in the wadi.

en.L: And Saul came to the city of Amalek and lay in wait in the wadi.
en.B: Saul advanced to the city of Amalek and lay in ambush in the ravine.
en.R: Saul went to the town of the Amalekites. He hid his men in a dry riverbed, ready to attack.

decisions.choice: lay in wait: set an ambush
decisions.reason: The vowels of the written form would suit a verb meaning "strove" or "fought", but the word is generally read as a form of the verb "lie in wait", which fits the place named: Saul hid his men in the valley before the attack.

decisions.choice: the wadi: a stream bed, dry except in the rainy season
decisions.reason: Such valleys cut deep through the dry south and gave cover for an army waiting to strike.

decisions.choice: the city of Amalek: an Amalekite settlement, not named
decisions.reason: The Amalekites were mostly herders who moved from place to place, but they also had settlements. This one is not named.

decisions.choice: He hid his men in a dry riverbed, ready to attack.
decisions.reason: Readable explains what an ambush is and what a wadi is (m1, m2).

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר שָׁא֣וּל אֶֽל־הַקֵּינִ֡י לְכוּ֩ סֻּ֨רוּ רְד֜וּ מִתּ֣וֹךְ עֲמָלֵקִ֗י פֶּן־אֹֽסִפְךָ֙ עִמּ֔וֹ וְאַתָּ֞ה עָשִׂ֤יתָה חֶ֨סֶד֙ עִם־כָּל־בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל בַּעֲלוֹתָ֖ם מִמִּצְרָ֑יִם וַיָּ֥סַר קֵינִ֖י מִתּ֥וֹךְ עֲמָלֵֽק׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Saul to the Kenites, go, turn aside, go down from among [the] Amalekites, lest I sweep you away with him; and you showed steadfast love to all [the] sons of Israel when they came up from Egypt. And turned aside [the] Kenites from among Amalek.

en.L: And Saul said to the Kenites, "Go, turn aside, go down from among the Amalekites, lest I sweep you away with them. For you showed steadfast love to all the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel when they came up from Egypt." And the Kenites turned aside from among Amalek.
en.B: Saul said to the Kenites, "Go, leave, get away from the Amalekites, or I will sweep you away along with them. For you showed faithful love to all the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} when they came up out of Egypt." So the Kenites moved away from the Amalekites.
en.R: Saul said to the Kenites, "Leave the Amalekites and go away from them. If you do not, I will destroy you along with them. You showed faithful love to all the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} when they came up out of Egypt." So the Kenites left the Amalekites.

decisions.choice: the Kenites: the clan of Moses' father-in-law
decisions.reason: The Kenites were a clan linked by marriage to Moses (Judges 1:16; 4:11). Some of them went with Israel from the wilderness and settled in the south among the people of Judah, near the Amalekites.

decisions.choice: steadfast love: loyal kindness beyond what was owed
decisions.reason: The word names faithful, loyal kindness. The Kenites had helped Israel in the wilderness: Moses asked Hobab to be Israel's "eyes" on the journey (Numbers 10:29-32). Saul repays that old kindness by sparing them.

decisions.choice: sweep you away: destroy you along with them
decisions.reason: The verb means to gather in or take away; here it means to remove by death, as a harvest is gathered (compare Psalm 26:9).

decisions.choice: steadfast love (Literal); faithful love (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: The book-wide wording for this word is kept, even though the love is shown by people and not by God (m2).

source.text: וַיַּ֥ךְ שָׁא֖וּל אֶת־עֲמָלֵ֑ק מֵֽחֲוִילָה֙ בּוֹאֲךָ֣ שׁ֔וּר אֲשֶׁ֖ר עַל־פְּנֵ֥י מִצְרָֽיִם׃

records.literal_gloss: And struck Saul Amalek from Havilah [as] your coming [to] Shur, which [is] on [the] face of Egypt.

en.L: And Saul struck Amalek from Havilah as you come to Shur, which [is] east of Egypt.
en.B: Then Saul struck down the Amalekites from Havilah all the way to Shur, which lies east of Egypt.
en.R: Then Saul defeated the Amalekites. He fought them from Havilah all the way to Shur, on the east side of Egypt.

decisions.choice: from Havilah to Shur: across the desert lands south of Israel
decisions.reason: The same words mark the lands of Ishmael's descendants in Genesis 25:18. Shur is the desert on Egypt's northeastern border (Genesis 16:7; Exodus 15:22). Where Havilah lay is not known for certain; it was somewhere in the desert to the east or southeast.

decisions.choice: as you come to Shur, which is on the face of Egypt: all the way to Shur, facing Egypt
decisions.reason: "As you come to" is a way of giving directions: on the road toward. "On the face of" means facing or next to; Shur lies on the edge of Egypt, on the side toward Israel, that is, to the east.

decisions.choice: all the way to; east of
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of the Hebrew directions (m2).

source.text: וַיִּתְפֹּ֛שׂ אֶת־אֲגַ֥ג מֶֽלֶךְ־עֲמָלֵ֖ק חָ֑י וְאֶת־כָּל־הָעָ֖ם הֶחֱרִ֥ים לְפִי־חָֽרֶב׃

records.literal_gloss: And seized Agag king of Amalek alive, and all the people he devoted to destruction by [the] mouth of [the] sword.

en.L: And he seized Agag king of Amalek alive, and all the people he devoted to destruction by the edge of the sword.
en.B: He captured Agag king of Amalek alive, and he devoted all the people to destruction with the sword.
en.R: He captured Agag, the king of the Amalekites, alive. But he destroyed all the people completely with the sword, as given over to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: Agag: the king of Amalek
decisions.reason: Balaam names Agag as a great king in Numbers 24:7, so the name may have been carried by more than one king of Amalek. Haman in Esther is called "the Agagite" (Esther 3:1), a descendant of this royal line.

decisions.choice: by the mouth of the sword: with the sword
decisions.reason: The sword is pictured as a mouth that devours; "by the mouth of the sword" means killed in battle with the sword.

decisions.choice: all the people: the Amalekites Saul's army met
decisions.reason: The words speak of the people Saul fought in this campaign. Amalekites appear again later (27:8; 30:1), so the account is not saying that none were left anywhere.

decisions.choice: destroyed ... completely, as given over to the LORD
decisions.reason: Readable explains the term as in verse 3. "But" sets the people's death against the sparing of Agag.

source.text: וַיַּחְמֹל֩ שָׁא֨וּל וְהָעָ֜ם עַל־אֲגָ֗ג וְעַל־מֵיטַ֣ב הַצֹּאן֩ וְהַבָּקָ֨ר וְהַמִּשְׁנִ֤ים וְעַל־הַכָּרִים֙ וְעַל־כָּל־הַטּ֔וֹב וְלֹ֥א אָב֖וּ הַחֲרִימָ֑ם וְכָל־הַמְּלָאכָ֛ה נְמִבְזָ֥ה וְנָמֵ֖ס אֹתָ֥הּ הֶחֱרִֽימוּ׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And spared Saul and the people Agag, and the best of the sheep and the cattle and the second ones and the lambs and all the good, and not they were willing to devote them to destruction; and all the property despised and worthless, it they devoted to destruction.

en.L: And Saul and the people spared Agag, and the best of the sheep and the cattle, and the fatlings and the lambs, and all that was good, and they were not willing to devote them to destruction. But all the property [that was] despised and worthless, that they devoted to destruction.
en.B: But Saul and the troops spared Agag. They also spared the finest sheep and cattle, the fattened animals and the lambs, and everything that was good. They were not willing to devote these to destruction. Everything that was despised and worthless they devoted to destruction.
en.R: But Saul and his army let Agag live. They also kept the best of the sheep and cattle, the fattest animals and the lambs, and everything else that was good. They did not want to destroy these things. They destroyed only what was weak or worthless.

decisions.choice: spared: had pity on, held back from destroying
decisions.reason: This is the verb of the command in verse 3, "do not spare him". The narrator uses the same word to show that Saul and the people did exactly what they were told not to do.

decisions.choice: the fatlings: animals of the best quality
alternatives: the animals of the second year
decisions.reason: The word means "second ones". It may name animals of the second birth or second year, thought to be the finest, or it may be a slip for a similar word meaning "fat ones". Either way, it names choice animals kept for their value.

decisions.choice: the property that was despised and worthless: whatever was not worth keeping
decisions.reason: The two descriptive words are unusual forms. The first means despised or of little value; the second probably means wasting away or weak. The contrast with "all that was good" is clear: they destroyed only what they did not want.

decisions.choice: they were not willing: a deliberate choice
decisions.reason: The verb expresses will and consent. Keeping the best was not an oversight in battle but a decision.

decisions.choice: the troops (Balanced); his army (Readable)
decisions.reason: "The people" are Saul's fighting men here (verse 4, m1). Literal keeps "the people".

source.text: וַֽיְהִי֙ דְּבַר־יְהוָ֔ה אֶל־שְׁמוּאֵ֖ל לֵאמֹֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: And came [the] word of Yahweh to Samuel, saying,

en.L: And the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} came to Samuel, saying,
en.B: Then the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} came to Samuel:
en.R: Then a message from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} came to Samuel:

decisions.choice: the word of the LORD came to Samuel: the LORD spoke to him as a prophet
decisions.reason: This is the usual way of saying that the LORD gave a prophet a message (3:1, 21; 2 Samuel 7:4). What follows is the LORD's own word about Saul.

decisions.choice: a message from the LORD
decisions.reason: Readable says "message" for "word", since the word is a whole message, not a single word.

source.text: נִחַ֗מְתִּי כִּֽי־הִמְלַ֤כְתִּי אֶת־שָׁאוּל֙ לְמֶ֔לֶךְ כִּֽי־שָׁב֙ מֵאַֽחֲרַ֔י וְאֶת־דְּבָרַ֖י לֹ֣א הֵקִ֑ים וַיִּ֨חַר֙ לִשְׁמוּאֵ֔ל וַיִּזְעַ֥ק אֶל־יְהוָ֖ה כָּל־הַלָּֽיְלָה׃

records.literal_gloss: I regret that I made king Saul as king, for he has turned back from after me, and my words not he has carried out. And it burned to Samuel, and he cried out to Yahweh all the night.

en.L: "I regret that I have made Saul king, for he has turned back from following {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} words he has not carried out." And Samuel was angry, and he cried out to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} all the night.
en.B: "I regret that I made Saul king, because he has turned back from following {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} and has failed to carry out {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} commands." Samuel was angry, and he cried out to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} all night long.
en.R: "I am sorry that I made Saul king. He has turned away from following {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and he has not done what I told him to do." Samuel was angry, and he cried out to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} all night.

decisions.choice: I regret: the LORD's sorrow and change of course, said in human terms
alternatives: I have changed my mind about making Saul king
I am grieved that I made Saul king
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used of God in Genesis 6:6 and Exodus 32:14: to be sorry, to grieve, to turn from a course once taken. This chapter uses it three times. The LORD regrets making Saul king (here and verse 35), and yet Samuel says that the Glory of Israel does not regret as a human does (verse 29). The writer sets these a few verses apart, so they are meant to be read together. Here the word speaks of God's grief at Saul's disobedience and of a real change in how he deals with Saul: the kingship given to him will not go on. It does not mean that God made a mistake he could not foresee; the loss of Saul's line had already been announced (13:13-14). Verse 29 adds that this sentence will not be reversed.

decisions.choice: turned back from following me: stopped being loyal to the LORD
decisions.reason: To "go after" someone is to follow and serve them as a loyal subject (12:14, 20). To turn back from following is to break that loyalty.

decisions.choice: my words he has not carried out: he has not done what I commanded
decisions.reason: The verb means to set up, to make stand, and with "words" it means to carry them out. Saul uses the same verb in verse 13 to claim that he has done just that.

decisions.choice: it burned to Samuel: Samuel was angry
decisions.reason: The phrase is the usual way of saying that someone became angry. The verse does not say at whom: at Saul's disobedience, or at the word he had received. The same phrase is used of David in 2 Samuel 6:8, where it may mean deep distress as much as anger.

decisions.choice: I regret (Literal, Balanced); I am sorry (Readable)
decisions.reason: The levels use words of regret and sorrow (m1). "Repent" is avoided at every level, since in English it suggests turning from sin. Readable uses the everyday "I am sorry".

decisions.choice: my commands (Balanced); what I told him to do (Readable)
decisions.reason: "My words" here are the LORD's commands about Amalek (m3).

source.text: וַיַּשְׁכֵּ֧ם שְׁמוּאֵ֛ל לִקְרַ֥את שָׁא֖וּל בַּבֹּ֑קֶר וַיֻּגַּ֨ד לִשְׁמוּאֵ֜ל לֵאמֹ֗ר בָּֽא־שָׁא֤וּל הַכַּרְמֶ֨לָה֙ וְהִנֵּ֨ה מַצִּ֥יב לוֹ֙ יָ֔ד וַיִּסֹּב֙ וַֽיַּעֲבֹ֔ר וַיֵּ֖רֶד הַגִּלְגָּֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: And rose early Samuel to meet Saul in the morning; and it was told to Samuel, saying, came Saul to Carmel, and look, [he is] setting up for himself a monument, and he turned and passed on and went down [to] Gilgal.

en.L: And Samuel rose early to meet Saul in the morning. And it was told to Samuel, saying, "Saul came to Carmel, and look, he was setting up a monument for himself, and he turned and passed on and went down to Gilgal."
en.B: Samuel got up early in the morning to meet Saul, and Samuel was told, "Saul went to Carmel and set up a monument for himself there. Then he turned and went on down to Gilgal."
en.R: Early the next morning Samuel got up to go and meet Saul. But someone told him, "Saul went to Carmel. He set up a monument there in his own honor. Then he left and went down to Gilgal."

decisions.choice: Carmel: a town in the hill country of Judah
decisions.reason: This Carmel lay south of Hebron (Joshua 15:55; 1 Samuel 25:2), on Saul's way back from the south. It is not Mount Carmel in the north.

decisions.choice: setting up a monument for himself: a memorial to his own victory
decisions.reason: The word is "hand", used of a standing stone or marker that keeps a name in memory (2 Samuel 18:18). "For himself" shows whom it honored. The report sets Saul's self-honor beside his neglect of the LORD's command.

decisions.choice: Gilgal: the place where Saul was made king
decisions.reason: At Gilgal the people had renewed Saul's kingship before the LORD (11:14-15), and there Saul had earlier gone against Samuel's word (13:8-14). Now he goes there to offer sacrifices (verse 21).

decisions.choice: set up a monument for himself there (Balanced); in his own honor (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable leave out "look", which marks something surprising in the report, and tell the steps in order. Readable says "in his own honor" for "for himself" (m2).

source.text: וַיָּבֹ֥א שְׁמוּאֵ֖ל אֶל־שָׁא֑וּל וַיֹּ֧אמֶר ל֣וֹ שָׁא֗וּל בָּר֤וּךְ אַתָּה֙ לַֽיהוָ֔ה הֲקִימֹ֖תִי אֶת־דְּבַ֥ר יְהוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And came Samuel to Saul, and said to him Saul, blessed [are] you to Yahweh; I have carried out [the] word of Yahweh.

en.L: And Samuel came to Saul, and Saul said to him, "Blessed [are] you to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}! I have carried out the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}."
en.B: When Samuel reached Saul, Saul greeted him, "May {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} bless you! I have carried out the command of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}."
en.R: When Samuel got there, Saul greeted him: "May {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} bless you! I have done what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} told me to do."

decisions.choice: blessed are you to the LORD: may the LORD bless you
decisions.reason: This is a greeting that is also a prayer for blessing (Ruth 2:20; 2 Samuel 2:5). Saul greets Samuel warmly, as if all were well.

decisions.choice: I have carried out: the verb the LORD used in verse 11
decisions.reason: The LORD had said, "my words he has not carried out". Saul claims, with the same verb, that he has. The reader already knows that his claim is false.

decisions.choice: the command of the LORD (Balanced); what the LORD told me to do (Readable)
decisions.reason: "The word of the LORD" here is the command about Amalek.

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר שְׁמוּאֵ֔ל וּמֶ֛ה קֽוֹל־הַצֹּ֥אן הַזֶּ֖ה בְּאָזְנָ֑י וְק֣וֹל הַבָּקָ֔ר אֲשֶׁ֥ר אָנֹכִ֖י שֹׁמֵֽעַ׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Samuel, and what [is] the sound of the sheep the this in my ears, and [the] sound of the cattle which I [am] hearing?

en.L: And Samuel said, "Then what [is] this sound of sheep in my ears, and the sound of cattle that I hear?"
en.B: Samuel replied, "Then what is this bleating of sheep that fills my ears, and the lowing of cattle that I can hear?"
en.R: But Samuel asked, "Then what is all this noise of sheep and cattle that I can hear?"

decisions.choice: sound: the word used for "voice" in "listen to the voice of the LORD"
decisions.reason: The word means both "sound" and "voice". Saul was told to listen to the voice of the LORD (verse 1), and now the voice of the animals he kept gives him away (compare verses 19, 22, 24).

decisions.choice: and what is this: a question that exposes the claim
decisions.reason: The question starts with "and": Saul says he has obeyed, and then what is this noise? It answers his claim without stating the charge.

decisions.choice: bleating; lowing
decisions.reason: Balanced uses the words for the sounds that sheep and cattle make. Literal keeps "sound" twice to show the link with "voice" (m1); Readable says "noise".

source.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר שָׁא֜וּל מֵעֲמָלֵקִ֣י הֱבִיא֗וּם אֲשֶׁ֨ר חָמַ֤ל הָעָם֙ עַל־מֵיטַ֤ב הַצֹּאן֙ וְהַבָּקָ֔ר לְמַ֥עַן זְבֹ֖חַ לַיהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֑יךָ וְאֶת־הַיּוֹתֵ֖ר הֶחֱרַֽמְנוּ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And said Saul, from [the] Amalekites they brought them, which spared the people the best of the sheep and the cattle so as to sacrifice to Yahweh your God; and the rest we devoted to destruction.

en.L: And Saul said, "They brought them from the Amalekites, for the people spared the best of the sheep and the cattle in order to sacrifice to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God. And the rest we devoted to destruction."
en.B: Saul answered, "They brought them from the Amalekites. The troops kept back the best of the sheep and cattle as sacrifices for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God, and everything else we devoted to destruction."
en.R: Saul answered, "The soldiers brought them from the Amalekites. They kept the best of the sheep and cattle to offer as sacrifices to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God. But we destroyed everything else completely, as given over to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}."

decisions.choice: they brought ... we devoted: Saul gives the blame to the people and keeps the credit
decisions.reason: Saul says "they" brought the animals and "the people" spared them, but "we" destroyed the rest. Verse 9 has already said that Saul and the people spared them together.

decisions.choice: the LORD your God: Saul speaks of the LORD as Samuel's God
decisions.reason: Saul says "your God" here and again in verses 21 and 30. It may be only a respectful way of speaking to a prophet, but beside his excuses it sounds distant, as if the LORD were Samuel's concern more than his own.

decisions.choice: for: the reason the animals were brought
decisions.reason: The connecting word can mean "which" or "because". Read as "because", it gives Saul's reason: the animals were kept for sacrifice.

decisions.choice: the troops / the soldiers; destroyed ... completely, as given over to the LORD (Readable)
decisions.reason: "The people" are the army (verse 4). Readable explains the term as in verse 3, so it names the LORD twice.

source.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר שְׁמוּאֵל֙ אֶל־שָׁא֔וּל הֶ֚רֶף וְאַגִּ֣ידָה לְּךָ֔ אֵת֩ אֲשֶׁ֨ר דִּבֶּ֧ר יְהוָ֛ה אֵלַ֖י הַלָּ֑יְלָה וַיֹּ֥אמֶר ל֖וֹ דַּבֵּֽר׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And said Samuel to Saul, stop, and let me tell you what spoke Yahweh to me the night. And he said to him, speak.

en.L: And Samuel said to Saul, "Stop, and let me tell you what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} spoke to me this night." And he said to him, "Speak."
en.B: "Enough!" Samuel said to Saul. "Let me tell you what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} told me during the night." "Go on," Saul answered.
en.R: "Stop!" Samuel said to Saul. "I will tell you what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} told me during the night." "Tell me," Saul said.

decisions.choice: stop: enough, say no more
decisions.reason: The verb means to let go or leave off. Samuel cuts short Saul's explanations.

decisions.choice: this night: the night just past
decisions.reason: "The night" is the night in which the LORD spoke and Samuel cried out (verses 10-11).

decisions.choice: he said: Saul answers
decisions.reason: The consonants as written give "they said"; the reading tradition of the Hebrew text has "he said", which is followed here. Either way it is Saul's side that answers "Speak".

decisions.choice: "Go on," Saul answered (Balanced); "Tell me," Saul said (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Saul as the speaker and give the single word "Speak" as "Go on" or "Tell me". Samuel's "Stop!" is put first, ahead of the speaker, to show how sharply he cuts Saul off.

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר שְׁמוּאֵ֔ל הֲל֗וֹא אִם־קָטֹ֤ן אַתָּה֙ בְּעֵינֶ֔יךָ רֹ֛אשׁ שִׁבְטֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל אָ֑תָּה וַיִּמְשָׁחֲךָ֧ יְהוָ֛ה לְמֶ֖לֶךְ עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Samuel, [is it] not, though small you [were] in your eyes, head of [the] tribes of Israel you [are]? And anointed you Yahweh as king over Israel.

en.L: And Samuel said, "Though you [were] small in your own eyes, [are] you not the head of the tribes of Israel? And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} anointed you king over Israel.
en.B: Samuel said, "Even if you were small in your own eyes, are you not head over the tribes of Israel? {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} anointed you as Israel's king.
en.R: Samuel said, "You once thought you were not important. But you are the leader of the tribes of Israel! {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} anointed you as king over Israel.

decisions.choice: small in your own eyes: Saul's humble beginning
decisions.reason: Samuel recalls how Saul spoke of himself when he was first chosen: from the smallest tribe and the least of its clans (9:21), and hiding among the baggage on the day he was named king (10:22). The LORD raised him from that.

decisions.choice: are you not the head: a question that expects "yes"
decisions.reason: The question reminds Saul of his position and so of his duty. As head of the tribes, he could not hide behind what the people wanted (verse 24).

decisions.choice: But you are the leader of the tribes of Israel!
decisions.reason: Readable turns the question into the statement it implies (m2) and says "leader" for "head".

source.text: וַיִּשְׁלָחֲךָ֥ יְהוָ֖ה בְּדָ֑רֶךְ וַיֹּ֗אמֶר לֵ֣ךְ וְהַחֲרַמְתָּ֞ה אֶת־הַֽחַטָּאִים֙ אֶת־עֲמָלֵ֔ק וְנִלְחַמְתָּ֣ ב֔וֹ עַ֥ד כַּלּוֹתָ֖ם אֹתָֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And sent you Yahweh on a way and said, go and devote to destruction the sinners, Amalek, and fight against him until finishing them.

en.L: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} sent you on a journey and said, 'Go, and devote to destruction the sinners, Amalek, and fight against them until you have finished them off.'
en.B: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} sent you on a mission and said, 'Go and devote to destruction those sinners, the Amalekites. Fight against them until you have wiped them out.'
en.R: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} sent you on a mission. He told you, 'Go and destroy those sinful Amalekites completely, as given over to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. Fight against them until they are all gone.'

decisions.choice: the sinners: a people under judgment for their wrongs
decisions.reason: The LORD's command is a sentence for what Amalek had done (verse 2), not a war for land or plunder. The word is used of the people of Sodom in Genesis 13:13.

decisions.choice: until finishing them: until Amalek has been wiped out
decisions.reason: The Hebrew form is unusual, something like "until their finishing them". It is best read as "until you have finished them off", the goal of the campaign.

decisions.choice: on a way: on a mission
decisions.reason: "Way" here is a journey with a purpose, an errand the LORD gave. Saul uses the same word in verse 20.

decisions.choice: mission; those sinners / those sinful Amalekites
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "mission" for "way" (m3). Readable explains the command as in verse 3.

source.text: וְלָ֥מָּה לֹא־שָׁמַ֖עְתָּ בְּק֣וֹל יְהוָ֑ה וַתַּ֨עַט֙ אֶל־הַשָּׁלָ֔ל וַתַּ֥עַשׂ הָרַ֖ע בְּעֵינֵ֥י יְהוָֽה׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And why not did you listen to [the] voice of Yahweh, and you swooped on the plunder and did the evil in [the] eyes of Yahweh?

en.L: And why did you not listen to the voice of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, but swooped on the plunder and did the evil in the eyes of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}?"
en.B: Why did you not obey the voice of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}? Why did you pounce on the plunder and do what was evil in the sight of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}?"
en.R: Why did you not obey {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}? Why did you rush to grab the plunder? You did what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said was evil."

decisions.choice: swooped on the plunder: rushed greedily at it
decisions.reason: The verb is used of a bird of prey diving on its food. The people had done the same in 14:32, when they swooped on the plunder after the battle with the Philistines.

decisions.choice: did the evil in the eyes of the LORD: did what the LORD judges to be evil
decisions.reason: This is the phrase used of Israel's unfaithfulness throughout Judges (Judges 2:11). Saul has acted like the generations whose ways the kingdom was meant to change.

decisions.choice: obey; did what was evil in the sight of (Balanced) / did what the LORD said was evil (Readable)
decisions.reason: "Listen to the voice" means obey (verse 1). The Judges wording for "did the evil in the eyes of" is kept at each level. Balanced and Readable split the question into two.

source.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר שָׁא֜וּל אֶל־שְׁמוּאֵ֗ל אֲשֶׁ֤ר שָׁמַ֨עְתִּי֙ בְּק֣וֹל יְהוָ֔ה וָאֵלֵ֕ךְ בַּדֶּ֖רֶךְ אֲשֶׁר־שְׁלָחַ֣נִי יְהוָ֑ה וָאָבִ֗יא אֶת־אֲגַג֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ עֲמָלֵ֔ק וְאֶת־עֲמָלֵ֖ק הֶחֱרַֽמְתִּי׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Saul to Samuel, that I listened to [the] voice of Yahweh, and I went on the way which sent me Yahweh, and I brought Agag king of Amalek, and Amalek I devoted to destruction.

en.L: And Saul said to Samuel, "But I did listen to the voice of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}! And I went on the journey on which {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} sent me, and I brought Agag king of Amalek, and Amalek I devoted to destruction.
en.B: Saul said to Samuel, "But I did obey the voice of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}! I went on the mission {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} sent me on. I brought back Agag king of Amalek, and I devoted the Amalekites to destruction.
en.R: Saul said to Samuel, "But I did obey {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}! I went where {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} sent me. I brought back Agag, the king of the Amalekites, and I destroyed the Amalekites completely, as given over to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: but I did listen: Saul protests
decisions.reason: The small word that begins Saul's reply often introduces a protest: "but I did". Saul does not accept Samuel's charge.

decisions.choice: I brought Agag ... and Amalek I devoted: Saul sees no wrong in sparing the king
decisions.reason: Saul puts the captured king side by side with the destruction of Amalek, as if bringing Agag back alive were part of obeying. The command of verse 3 had spared no one.

decisions.choice: obey; mission (Balanced); went where the LORD sent me, destroyed ... completely (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in verses 18-19. Readable explains the term as in verse 3.

source.text: וַיִּקַּ֨ח הָעָ֧ם מֵהַשָּׁלָ֛ל צֹ֥אן וּבָקָ֖ר רֵאשִׁ֣ית הַחֵ֑רֶם לִזְבֹּ֛חַ לַֽיהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֶ֖יךָ בַּגִּלְגָּֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: And took the people from the plunder sheep and cattle, [the] first of the devoted thing, to sacrifice to Yahweh your God in Gilgal.

en.L: And the people took from the plunder sheep and cattle, the first of the devoted things, to sacrifice to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God in Gilgal."
en.B: From the plunder the troops took sheep and cattle, the choicest of what was devoted to destruction, to sacrifice to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God at Gilgal."
en.R: The soldiers took sheep and cattle from the plunder. They chose the best of the animals that belonged to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and should have been destroyed. They wanted to offer them as sacrifices to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God at Gilgal."

decisions.choice: the first of: the choicest part
decisions.reason: The word means the first or best part, the word used for the firstfruits that belong to God (Deuteronomy 18:4). Saul presents the animals as the LORD's best share.

decisions.choice: the devoted things offered as sacrifices: an offering that was not Israel's to give
decisions.reason: What is devoted already belongs wholly to the LORD and cannot be redeemed or used (Leviticus 27:28-29). The command was to destroy these animals, not to offer them. To sacrifice them is to give God what was already his while keeping the honor of the gift, and it also meant a feast for the people, since many sacrifices were eaten.

decisions.choice: the devoted thing: everything put under the ban
decisions.reason: The singular noun names the whole body of what was devoted (as in Joshua 7:1).

decisions.choice: the animals that belonged to the LORD and should have been destroyed
decisions.reason: Readable explains "the devoted things" (m2, m3) and says "They wanted to" to show the purpose.

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר שְׁמוּאֵ֗ל הַחֵ֤פֶץ לַֽיהוָה֙ בְּעֹל֣וֹת וּזְבָחִ֔ים כִּשְׁמֹ֖עַ בְּק֣וֹל יְהוָ֑ה הִנֵּ֤ה שְׁמֹ֨עַ֙ מִזֶּ֣בַח ט֔וֹב לְהַקְשִׁ֖יב מֵחֵ֥לֶב אֵילִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Samuel, [is there] delight to Yahweh in burnt offerings and sacrifices as in listening to [the] voice of Yahweh? Look, to listen than sacrifice [is] good, to pay attention than [the] fat of rams.

en.L: And Samuel said, "Does {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} [have] delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices \q as in listening to the voice of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}? \q Look, to listen [is] better than sacrifice, \q to pay attention than the fat of rams.
en.B: Samuel said, "Is {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} as pleased with burnt offerings and sacrifices \q as with obeying the voice of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}? \q See, to obey is better than sacrifice, \q and to pay heed is better than the fat of rams.
en.R: Samuel said, "Does {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} enjoy burnt offerings and sacrifices \q as much as {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} enjoys being obeyed? \q No! It is better to obey than to offer sacrifices. \q It is better to listen to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} than to offer the fat of rams.

decisions.choice: does the LORD delight ... as in listening: a question that expects "no"
decisions.reason: The question is not about whether sacrifice pleases God at all; it compares two things. Obeying his voice pleases him more, as the second half of the verse says outright.

decisions.choice: burnt offerings, sacrifices, the fat of rams
decisions.reason: A burnt offering was burned whole on the altar; other sacrifices were shared in a meal, with the fat burned for the LORD as his portion (Leviticus 3:9-11, 16). "The fat of rams" is the best part of the best animals.

decisions.choice: to listen is better than sacrifice: worship cannot stand in for obedience
decisions.reason: Samuel does not reject the sacrifices the Law commands. He says that offerings made instead of obedience do not please God. The prophets say the same again and again (Hosea 6:6; Amos 5:21-24; Isaiah 1:11-17; Jeremiah 7:21-23; Psalm 40:7-9).

decisions.choice: to pay attention: to listen closely and heed
decisions.reason: The verb, used beside "listen", means to turn the ear and take notice; it repeats the first half of the saying in other words.

decisions.choice: Samuel's reply is poetry
decisions.reason: Samuel's answer (verses 22-23) is set in balanced pairs of lines, as prophets' sayings often are.

decisions.choice: obeying / to obey (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: "Listen to the voice" means obey (verse 1), so Balanced and Readable say "obey". Literal keeps "listen" to show the play on "voice" and "sound" in verses 14, 19 and 24.

decisions.choice: No!
decisions.reason: Readable answers the question, as the second half of the verse does (m1), in place of "look".

source.text: כִּ֤י חַטַּאת־קֶ֨סֶם֙ מֶ֔רִי וְאָ֥וֶן וּתְרָפִ֖ים הַפְצַ֑ר יַ֗עַן מָאַ֨סְתָּ֙ אֶת־דְּבַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה וַיִּמְאָסְךָ֖ מִמֶּֽלֶךְ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: For [the] sin of divination [is] rebellion, and iniquity and teraphim [is] presumption. Because you rejected [the] word of Yahweh, and he rejected you from king.

en.L: For rebellion [is] the sin of divination, \q and presumption [is] iniquity and household gods. \q Because you have rejected the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has rejected you from [being] king."
en.B: For rebellion is as sinful as divination, \q and arrogance is like wickedness and household gods. \q You have rejected the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q so {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has rejected you as king."
en.R: Refusing to obey is as sinful as trying to learn the future by magic. \q Being proud and stubborn is as evil as worshiping household idols. \q You have rejected what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} told you, \q so {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has rejected you as king."

decisions.choice: rebellion is the sin of divination: rebellion is as bad as divination
decisions.reason: The lines set two things side by side with no verb. They do not say that rebellion is the same act as divination, but that it is just as serious a sin before God.

decisions.choice: divination: seeking hidden knowledge by omens and signs
decisions.reason: Divination was forbidden in Israel (Deuteronomy 18:10-14). Later Saul himself will seek a medium to call up Samuel (28:7-8).

decisions.choice: iniquity and household gods: wickedness linked with idols
decisions.reason: The first word means wrongdoing, and it is often used of idol worship (Hosea 10:8). Teraphim were small images of household gods (Genesis 31:19; 1 Samuel 19:13). The pair names idolatry.

decisions.choice: presumption: pushing ahead with one's own will
decisions.reason: The word comes from a verb meaning to press or urge (Genesis 19:3; 33:11). It describes insisting on one's own way against what God has said.

decisions.choice: you have rejected ... he has rejected you: the sentence matches the deed
decisions.reason: The same verb is used twice. Saul refused the LORD's word, and the LORD refuses Saul as king. Verse 26 repeats it.

decisions.choice: as sinful as; arrogance is like (Balanced); as evil as (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable state the comparison the lines imply (m1). Balanced says "arrogance" and Readable "being proud and stubborn" for the rare word (m4). Balanced joins the last two lines with "so" in place of "because", which says the same thing.

decisions.choice: trying to learn the future by magic; worshiping household idols
decisions.reason: Readable explains "divination" and uses the book-wide Readable wording for teraphim, "household idols".

source.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר שָׁא֤וּל אֶל־שְׁמוּאֵל֙ חָטָ֔אתִי כִּֽי־עָבַ֥רְתִּי אֶת־פִּֽי־יְהוָ֖ה וְאֶת־דְּבָרֶ֑יךָ כִּ֤י יָרֵ֨אתִי֙ אֶת־הָעָ֔ם וָאֶשְׁמַ֖ע בְּקוֹלָֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Saul to Samuel, I have sinned, for I transgressed [the] mouth of Yahweh and your words, because I feared the people and listened to their voice.

en.L: And Saul said to Samuel, "I have sinned, for I have transgressed the mouth of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and your words, because I feared the people and listened to their voice.
en.B: Then Saul said to Samuel, "I have sinned. I have broken the command of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and your instructions, because I was afraid of the troops and gave in to what they said.
en.R: Then Saul said to Samuel, "I have sinned. I did not keep the command of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} or follow your instructions. I was afraid of my soldiers, so I did what they wanted.

decisions.choice: transgressed the mouth of the LORD: broke the LORD's command
decisions.reason: "Mouth" stands for what was spoken, a command. To "pass over" it is to go beyond it, to break it.

decisions.choice: listened to their voice: obeyed the people
decisions.reason: Saul now admits that he listened to the wrong voice. The chapter set listening to the voice of the LORD (verses 1, 19, 20, 22) against this.

decisions.choice: I have sinned ... because I feared the people: a confession with an excuse
decisions.reason: Saul confesses, but he also gives a reason that shifts part of the blame, as in verse 15. The king, who is "head of the tribes" (verse 17), says he gave way to fear of his own troops.

decisions.choice: the troops / my soldiers; gave in to what they said / did what they wanted
decisions.reason: "The people" are the army (verse 4). Balanced and Readable give the sense of "listened to their voice" (m2); Literal keeps the word "voice".

source.text: וְעַתָּ֕ה שָׂ֥א נָ֖א אֶת־חַטָּאתִ֑י וְשׁ֣וּב עִמִּ֔י וְאֶֽשְׁתַּחֲוֶ֖ה לַֽיהוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And now, forgive please my sin, and return with me, and I will bow down to Yahweh.

en.L: And now, please forgive my sin, and return with me, that I may bow down to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}."
en.B: Now please forgive my sin, and come back with me so that I may worship {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}."
en.R: Now please forgive my sin. Come back with me so that I can worship {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}."

decisions.choice: forgive: bear away, pardon
decisions.reason: The verb means to lift up or carry; with "sin" it means to take it away, to pardon. Saul asks Samuel to pardon him, or to stand with him so that he is seen as pardoned.

decisions.choice: bow down: worship
decisions.reason: The verb means to bow low to the ground, the bodily act of worship.

decisions.choice: return with me: come back and worship with me in public
decisions.reason: Saul wants the prophet beside him when he worships at Gilgal, where the people and the elders can see it (verse 30).

decisions.choice: worship
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "worship" for the act of bowing down (m2); Literal keeps "bow down".

source.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר שְׁמוּאֵל֙ אֶל־שָׁא֔וּל לֹ֥א אָשׁ֖וּב עִמָּ֑ךְ כִּ֤י מָאַ֨סְתָּה֙ אֶת־דְּבַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה וַיִּמְאָסְךָ֣ יְהוָ֔ה מִהְי֥וֹת מֶ֖לֶךְ עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And said Samuel to Saul, not I will return with you, for you have rejected [the] word of Yahweh, and rejected you Yahweh from being king over Israel.

en.L: And Samuel said to Saul, "I will not return with you, for you have rejected the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has rejected you from being king over Israel."
en.B: But Samuel said to Saul, "I will not go back with you. You have rejected the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has rejected you as king over Israel."
en.R: But Samuel said to Saul, "I will not go back with you. You have rejected what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} told you. So {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has rejected you. You will no longer be king over Israel."

decisions.choice: you have rejected ... the LORD has rejected you: Samuel repeats the sentence of verse 23
decisions.reason: Samuel restates the verdict in plain words: the rejection matches the deed. Saul's request does not change it.

decisions.choice: from being king: so that you are no longer king
decisions.reason: The words say what Saul is rejected from. The sentence is on his reign as the LORD's king; he will still hold the throne for years, but the LORD no longer stands behind his kingship (16:1, 14).

decisions.choice: So the LORD has rejected you. You will no longer be king over Israel.
decisions.reason: Readable breaks the sentence into short ones and states what "rejected you from being king" means (m2).

source.text: וַיִּסֹּ֥ב שְׁמוּאֵ֖ל לָלֶ֑כֶת וַיַּחֲזֵ֥ק בִּכְנַף־מְעִיל֖וֹ וַיִּקָּרַֽע׃

records.literal_gloss: And turned Samuel to go, and he seized [the] hem of his robe, and it tore.

en.L: And Samuel turned to go, and he took hold of the hem of his robe, and it tore.
en.B: As Samuel turned to leave, Saul caught hold of the hem of his robe, and it tore.
en.R: Samuel turned to leave, but Saul grabbed the edge of Samuel's robe, and it tore.

decisions.choice: he seized: Saul took hold of Samuel's robe
alternatives: Samuel took hold of the hem of Saul's robe
decisions.reason: The Hebrew does not name the one who seized the robe. The setting shows that it was Saul, holding Samuel back as he turned to go, and the ancient Greek translation names Saul here. Some have read it as Samuel tearing Saul's robe as a sign, but verse 28 reads best as Samuel explaining what had just happened to his own robe.

decisions.choice: the hem of his robe: the edge of the prophet's cloak
decisions.reason: The robe was an outer garment of some standing; Samuel wore one from childhood (2:19), and Saul will know him by it (28:14). Grasping a person's hem was a gesture of pleading. Later David will cut off the hem of Saul's robe (24:5).

decisions.choice: Saul (Balanced, Readable); Samuel's robe (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Saul as the one who took hold of the robe (m1); Readable also names Samuel as its owner. Literal keeps the Hebrew "he" and "his".

source.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֵלָיו֙ שְׁמוּאֵ֔ל קָרַ֨ע יְהוָ֜ה אֶֽת־מַמְלְכ֧וּת יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל מֵעָלֶ֖יךָ הַיּ֑וֹם וּנְתָנָ֕הּ לְרֵעֲךָ֖ הַטּ֥וֹב מִמֶּֽךָּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And said to him Samuel, has torn Yahweh [the] kingdom of Israel from upon you the day, and has given it to your neighbor, the good [one] more than you.

en.L: And Samuel said to him, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day, and has given it to your neighbor, who [is] better than you.
en.B: Then Samuel told him, "Today {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has torn the kingdom of Israel away from you and has given it to one of your neighbors, one better than you.
en.R: Samuel said to him, "Today {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has torn the kingdom of Israel away from you. He has given it to another man, one who is better than you.

decisions.choice: has torn: the torn robe is a sign
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used of the robe in verse 27. What happened to Samuel's robe pictures what the LORD has done to Saul's kingdom. The prophet Ahijah will tear a robe as a sign of a divided kingdom in 1 Kings 11:29-31.

decisions.choice: has given it: the decision is made, though not yet seen
decisions.reason: The verb is in the form for a finished act. The new king has not yet been anointed (16:1-13), but in the LORD's purpose the kingdom already belongs to him.

decisions.choice: your neighbor, better than you: another Israelite, not yet named
decisions.reason: The word means a neighbor or fellow, someone of Saul's own people. It is David (16:13), and 28:17 repeats these words with his name.

decisions.choice: another man
decisions.reason: Readable says "another man" for "your neighbor", which here means a fellow Israelite (m3), not someone living next door.

source.text: וְגַם֙ נֵ֣צַח יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל לֹ֥א יְשַׁקֵּ֖ר וְלֹ֣א יִנָּחֵ֑ם כִּ֣י לֹ֥א אָדָ֛ם ה֖וּא לְהִנָּחֵֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And also [the] Glory of Israel not will lie and not will regret, for not a man [is] he to regret.

en.L: And also the Glory of Israel will not lie and will not regret, for {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} [is] not {{gender:a human|a man}}, that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} should regret."
en.B: Moreover, the Glory of Israel will not lie or change {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} mind, for {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is not a mortal, that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} should change {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} mind."
en.R: Besides, God, the Glory of Israel, does not lie or change {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} mind. He is not a human being, who might change course."

decisions.choice: the Glory of Israel: a title of God
decisions.reason: The title is found only here. The noun can mean splendor, lasting strength, victory or endurance (it is used for "forever" in many places). Each sense fits a God whose word stands.

decisions.choice: he will not regret: God does not go back on his sentence, as a human might
alternatives: the two statements contradict each other
decisions.reason: This is the same verb as "I regret" in verse 11 and "the LORD regretted" in verse 35, and the words echo Balaam's in Numbers 23:19. The chapter holds both statements within a few verses. In verses 11 and 35 the word speaks of God's real grief at Saul's disobedience and of his turning from the course he had begun with Saul. Here Samuel denies that God changes his mind the way people do: by being fickle, by being deceived, or by being talked out of a decision. Saul has just pleaded to be restored (verses 25, 30); Samuel's answer is that the sentence of verse 28 will not be undone. So God's "regret" is his true response to what people do, not a sign of weakness or ignorance; and his word, once spoken in judgment, stands (compare Jeremiah 18:7-10, where God says he relents when people turn, and Exodus 32:14).

decisions.choice: not a man that he should regret: humans change their minds; God is not like them
decisions.reason: The line compares God with people. A human ruler might reverse a decree when begged; God's word does not bend that way.

decisions.choice: and also: Samuel adds a further reason
decisions.reason: The words add to verse 28: not only has the LORD torn the kingdom away; he will not take the sentence back.

decisions.choice: regret (Literal); change his mind (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "regret" here as in verses 11 and 35, so the reader can see that one verb is used three times. Balanced and Readable say "change his mind", the sense this verse denies (m2), while keeping "regret" and "was sorry" in verses 11 and 35.

decisions.choice: God, the Glory of Israel
decisions.reason: Readable names God, so that the unusual title is clearly a title of the LORD (m1).

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר חָטָ֔אתִי עַתָּ֗ה כַּבְּדֵ֥נִי נָ֛א נֶ֥גֶד זִקְנֵֽי־עַמִּ֖י וְנֶ֣גֶד יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וְשׁ֣וּב עִמִּ֔י וְהִֽשְׁתַּחֲוֵ֖יתִי לַֽיהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֶֽיךָ׃

records.literal_gloss: And he said, I have sinned; now honor me please before [the] elders of my people and before Israel, and return with me, and I will bow down to Yahweh your God.

en.L: And he said, "I have sinned. Now honor me, please, before the elders of my people and before Israel, and return with me, and I will bow down to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God."
en.B: Saul said, "I have sinned. But please honor me now in front of the elders of my people and in front of Israel. Return with me, and let me worship {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God."
en.R: Saul said, "I have sinned. But please show me respect in front of the leaders of my people and in front of the people of Israel. Come back with me so that I can worship {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God."

decisions.choice: I have sinned; now honor me: a confession followed by a request for honor
decisions.reason: Saul repeats his confession, but what he asks for now is honor before the people. His concern is how he will be seen.

decisions.choice: the LORD your God
decisions.reason: As in verses 15 and 21, Saul calls the LORD Samuel's God.

decisions.choice: Saul said; leaders (Readable); worship
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Saul as the speaker. Readable says "leaders" for "elders", the older men who led the tribes, and "the people of Israel"; Balanced and Readable say "worship" (verse 25).

source.text: וַיָּ֥שָׁב שְׁמוּאֵ֖ל אַחֲרֵ֣י שָׁא֑וּל וַיִּשְׁתַּ֥חוּ שָׁא֖וּל לַֽיהוָֽה׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And returned Samuel after Saul, and bowed down Saul to Yahweh.

en.L: And Samuel returned after Saul, and Saul bowed down to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.B: So Samuel went back with Saul, and Saul worshiped {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.R: So Samuel went back with Saul, and Saul worshiped {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: Samuel went back: the sentence still stands
decisions.reason: Samuel had refused to go back (verse 26), and now he does. He grants Saul honor before the people, but nothing in the verdict changes. He also has a duty of his own still to carry out: the sentence on Agag (verses 32-33).

decisions.choice: went back with; worshiped
decisions.reason: "Returned after Saul" means he followed Saul back. Balanced and Readable say "worshiped" for "bowed down" (verse 25).

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר שְׁמוּאֵ֗ל הַגִּ֤ישׁוּ אֵלַי֙ אֶת־אֲגַג֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ עֲמָלֵ֔ק וַיֵּ֣לֶךְ אֵלָ֔יו אֲגַ֖ג מַעֲדַנֹּ֑ת וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֲגָ֔ג אָכֵ֖ן סָ֥ר מַר־הַמָּֽוֶת׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And said Samuel, bring near to me Agag king of Amalek. And went to him Agag [in] delights, and said Agag, surely has turned aside [the] bitterness of the death.

en.L: And Samuel said, "Bring near to me Agag king of Amalek." And Agag came to him confidently. And Agag said, "Surely the bitterness of death has turned aside."
en.B: Then Samuel said, "Bring Agag king of Amalek here to me." Agag came to him confidently, and Agag said, "Surely the bitterness of death is past."
en.R: Then Samuel said, "Bring me Agag, the king of the Amalekites." Agag came to him full of hope. He said, "Surely the bitter threat of death is over for me now."

decisions.choice: confidently: at ease, expecting to be spared
decisions.reason: The word is rare. Taken from a root meaning "delight", it means cheerfully or at ease, and fits Agag's words that follow. With the letters read in a slightly different order, it means "in bonds" (compare Job 38:31), and some take it as "trembling" or "reluctantly".

decisions.choice: surely the bitterness of death has passed: Agag thinks he is safe
decisions.reason: Read this way, Agag believes that since he has been kept alive so far, he will not now be killed. The ancient Greek translation has a different sense, "Is death as bitter as this?", and some read the Hebrew as "Surely death is bitter", Agag's lament as he comes to die.

decisions.choice: full of hope; the bitter threat of death is over for me now
decisions.reason: Readable makes plain what Agag's confidence and words mean (m1, m2).

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר שְׁמוּאֵ֔ל כַּאֲשֶׁ֨ר שִׁכְּלָ֤ה נָשִׁים֙ חַרְבֶּ֔ךָ כֵּן־תִּשְׁכַּ֥ל מִנָּשִׁ֖ים אִמֶּ֑ךָ וַיְשַׁסֵּ֨ף שְׁמוּאֵ֧ל אֶת־אֲגָ֛ג לִפְנֵ֥י יְהוָ֖ה בַּגִּלְגָּֽל׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And said Samuel, as made childless women your sword, so will be childless from women your mother. And hewed in pieces Samuel Agag before Yahweh in Gilgal.

en.L: And Samuel said, "As your sword has made women childless, so your mother shall be childless among women." And Samuel hewed Agag in pieces before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} in Gilgal.
en.B: But Samuel said, "Just as your sword has robbed women of their children, so your mother will be robbed of her child among women." And Samuel cut Agag to pieces before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} at Gilgal.
en.R: But Samuel said, "Your sword has taken away the children of many mothers. Now your mother will lose her child too." Then Samuel cut Agag into pieces in front of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} at Gilgal.

decisions.choice: as your sword has made women childless: Agag's death is a judgment on his own violence
decisions.reason: Samuel names Agag's own deeds as the ground of the sentence. What he did to others' children is done to him, and the command of verse 3 is carried out.

decisions.choice: hewed in pieces: put to death by the sword
decisions.reason: The verb occurs only here. It seems to mean cutting in pieces, a violent execution.

decisions.choice: before the LORD in Gilgal: at the sanctuary, as an act of judgment
decisions.reason: Gilgal was a place of worship (verses 12, 21). The execution is carried out in the LORD's presence as his sentence, not as private revenge.

decisions.choice: robbed women of their children (Balanced); taken away the children of many mothers (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable spell out "made childless" and "childless among women". Readable adds "too", the link the verse implies.

source.text: וַיֵּ֥לֶךְ שְׁמוּאֵ֖ל הָרָמָ֑תָה וְשָׁא֛וּל עָלָ֥ה אֶל־בֵּית֖וֹ גִּבְעַ֥ת שָׁאֽוּל׃

records.literal_gloss: And went Samuel [to] Ramah, and Saul went up to his house [at] Gibeah of Saul.

en.L: And Samuel went to Ramah, and Saul went up to his house at Gibeah of Saul.
en.B: Then Samuel went to Ramah, and Saul went up to his home at Gibeah of Saul.
en.R: Then Samuel went to Ramah, and Saul went up to his home in Gibeah, the town where he lived.

decisions.choice: Ramah and Gibeah of Saul: each man's home
decisions.reason: Ramah was Samuel's home (7:17). Gibeah, in Benjamin, was Saul's home town and royal seat, and so it was called "Gibeah of Saul" (10:26; 11:4). The two men part and go their own ways.

decisions.choice: Gibeah, the town where he lived
decisions.reason: Readable explains "Gibeah of Saul" (m1).

source.text: וְלֹא־יָסַ֨ף שְׁמוּאֵ֜ל לִרְא֤וֹת אֶת־שָׁאוּל֙ עַד־י֣וֹם מוֹת֔וֹ כִּֽי־הִתְאַבֵּ֥ל שְׁמוּאֵ֖ל אֶל־שָׁא֑וּל וַיהוָ֣ה נִחָ֔ם כִּֽי־הִמְלִ֥יךְ אֶת־שָׁא֖וּל עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And not again Samuel to see Saul until [the] day of his death, for mourned Samuel for Saul; and Yahweh regretted that he had made king Saul over Israel.

en.L: And Samuel did not see Saul again until the day of his death, though Samuel mourned for Saul. And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} regretted that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had made Saul king over Israel.
en.B: Samuel did not go to see Saul again until the day he died, though Samuel grieved over Saul. And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} regretted having made Saul king over Israel.
en.R: Samuel did not go to see Saul again until the day he died. But Samuel was sad about Saul. And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} was sorry that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had made Saul king over Israel.

decisions.choice: did not see again: did not come to see Saul
alternatives: until the day of Saul's death
decisions.reason: Saul later comes to where Samuel is (19:22-24), but Samuel never again goes to Saul as his prophet. "His death" is most likely Samuel's own; Samuel died before Saul (25:1), and Saul then sought him through a medium (28:11-19).

decisions.choice: though: Samuel grieved even as he stayed away
decisions.reason: The linking word can mean "for" or "but". Read as "for", Samuel stayed away because he was mourning Saul as one already lost. Read as "though", he kept away and yet grieved. Both show a real sorrow over Saul.

decisions.choice: the LORD regretted: as in verse 11
decisions.reason: The chapter closes with the word it began with (verse 11; see the note there and at verse 29). God's grief over Saul and the end of his favor to Saul's reign stand together with his refusal to take back the sentence.

decisions.choice: regretted (Literal, Balanced); was sorry (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in verse 11.
